title: Scaffolding, Culture and Theories of Action
author: Nickhart, Mr.
summary: Scaffolding has come to be the fashionable term for how teachers ensure that children can access the curriculum. Often, the term is used to describe supporting children who might need more help and it is commonly used synonymously with differentiation. It is tempting to consider whether they are the same thing but I'm not sure that this is the right question to be asking. The names that we give to such teaching practices are only important in their representation of shared conceptual understanding, whether that is within a school or across the education system. That shared conceptual understanding is more important than the terminology it represents. Consider this model for understanding culture: Schein's model makes clear the difference between the superficial features of a school's culture and what is less visible. If we take the example of differentiation / scaffolding and look closely at what happens in lessons for children that need additional support to access the curriculum, one might see any number cultural artefacts, including, for example: Classrooms of children across the school, set by perceived ability based on past assessments Tables of children in a classroom, organised by perceived ability based on past assessments Children being given different work to complete based on the teacher's judgement of what they might be able to achieve Teaching assistants sitting with certain children, supporting them to do their work Flexible grouping of children based on the extent to which they have understood what they are working on in that lesson All children doing similar work but supported by adults to access it where needed The cultural artefacts visible around the school in relation to supporting children to access the curriculum are only there because they have been deliberately chosen by teachers or leaders. That choice is a result of the leaders' or teachers' beliefs about children's ability to learn what is expected of them. Claire Stoneman wrote recently about improving school visits by, among other things, being wary of novelty and making deeper structures visible. The same principle applies to learning from each other in the realm of differentiation / scaffolding. When we see other schools doing interesting work around differentiation or scaffolding, or hear from others developing thinking in this area, it is tempting to want to replicate them. This is arguably one of the most ubiquitous of implementation errors in schools, neatly summarised by Dylan William: Everything works somewhere; nothing works everywhere. Mimicking the cultural artefacts of another school could might work brilliantly if the underlying beliefs match. If we take it as a given that a school leader understands the intricacies of differentiation / scaffolding very well, strategies like this succeed or fail based on leaders' knowledge of their own school content. That context has to take into account the underlying beliefs that staff hold either collectively or individually. Viviane Robinson calls this understanding others' theories of action: If leaders are seeking to manage change, for example by improving their work around differentiation or scaffolding, and focus their efforts on the actions that they want to see from teachers, they will only succeed if the new actions expected of teachers are aligned with their key beliefs or values. Robinson argues that the target of change needs to be teachers' underlying beliefs, not what we want them to do. In the case of differentiation / scaffolding, key beliefs might be built around: Teachers' opinions on whether intelligence is fixed Teachers' expectations of what children are capable of Teachers' opinions on what makes great teaching Teachers' opinions on what TAs should be doing For example, if a teacher thinks that there are a group of children in their class that will never catch up with the curriculum or their peers, they may be reluctant to switch from a 'making the work easier' mindset to one of higher expectations and unlikely to implement any attempt to scaffold instead. If a teacher thinks that great teaching is differentiating work at least five ways and anything less does not cater for children's diverse needs, they'll never be behind homogeneity of expectation supported by scaffolding. Robinson suggests that in order to influence teachers' beliefs, they need to engage teachers' theories of action. Essentially, this requires plenty of discussion and probably some sort of evidence that the teacher finds acceptable. Of course, this requires leaders to have a clear idea of their own theory of action. When it comes to differentiation and scaffolding, these are mine: A scaffold is a way of adapting a task that enables all to access it, specifically: Every child joins a lesson with different prior knowledge and therefore requires different amounts of time and practice to become fluent in a procedure. If we do not allow enough time for particularly the most vulnerable children, we condemn them to incomplete understanding. Children should be given the opportunity to work without scaffolds. Children with different levels of prior knowledge might need different instruction. Scaffolds should increase the likelihood of children experiencing success in challenging tasks. Scaffolding can be through carefully chosen responses to children while they're working.
